deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a history-of-science excerpt in English, copied by hand under a German heading: 'Widerstand des Cartesianismus gegen Newton's Principien' (Resistance of Cartesianism to Newton's Principia). The text matches David Brewster's 'The Life of Sir Isaac Newton' (1831), in the chapter on how the Principia was received. The page references p. 174 and p. 179 point to that book.

Content, in order:
(1) Cartesian vortex theory dominated Europe. It appealed to the imagination through the analogy of bodies swirling in whirlpools. Riemann adds German glosses above 'eddies' (Wirbel) and 'whirlpool' (Mahlstrom).
(2) Because of this, the Principia was received with distrust. Even capable mathematicians saw gravitation as a revival of occult qualities. The parenthetical list of resisters is Leibniz, Huygens, Johann Bernoulli, Mairan, Cassini and Maraldi, and Fontenelle.
(3) Early continental adopters were Louville (before 1720), 's Gravesande in the Dutch universities (somewhat earlier) and Maupertuis (after visiting England in 1728). Despite them, Voltaire's remark stands: at Newton's death he had no more than twenty followers outside England.
(4) On England, Brewster contests Playfair's account, which is cited only by ellipses ('p. 174 ... p. 179 ...'). Brewster's conclusion is that the mathematical doctrines were taught academically from the start. Within twenty years the physical truths were popularised through experimental lectures, footnoted as John Keill at Oxford (1704/05 to 1710) and Desaguliers at Oxford (1710 to 1713). Cartesianism lingered in the universities only briefly; the next page completes the sentence.

These are reading notes or excerpts, presumably gathered for Riemann's natural-philosophy studies on action at a distance versus a medium. They contain no derivation to reconstruct.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics.

Copying slips in the excerpt: 'compels us a different view' is missing a verb (Brewster presumably has 'compels us to take a different view'), and 'accommodated to the to the capacities' is a dittography.

Historical precision of the copied claim: the Principia appeared in July 1687 and Newton died in March 1727 (Gregorian calendar). He therefore survived the publication by just under 40 years, not 'more than forty'. This follows Voltaire's and Brewster's rounding.

Keill's experimental-philosophy lectures at Oxford are usually dated earlier, from the late 1690s. The dates '1704 or 1705' are Brewster's, and Riemann's own hesitation ('1704 or 1705') reflects that uncertainty.

results.what: Excerpt on the Cartesian resistance to Newton's Principia and the spread of Newtonianism (Voltaire's 'twenty followers' remark; Keill and Desaguliers as popularisers)
results.modern_name: History of the reception of Newtonianism (Cartesian vortex theory vs. universal gravitation)
results.usually_credited_to: David Brewster, The Life of Sir Isaac Newton (1831); also Playfair's Dissertation (Encyclopaedia Britannica supplement)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a verbatim reading excerpt from Brewster's biography of Newton with a few German glosses. It contains no original mathematics or physics. It mainly shows that Riemann read Brewster's Newton, which fits his known interest in action at a distance and ether theories.

checkable.asserts: Calendar-year difference between the Principia (1687) and Newton's death (1727) is 40. The actual interval, July 1687 to March 1727, is slightly under 40 years, so 'more than forty' is a rounding.
Duration of Desaguliers' Oxford lecturing per the footnote is 3 years.

transcription_corrections: The illegible gloss '{+[?]+}' written above the struck-out 'Dutch' appears to be German 'holländ.' / 'holländischen' (Dutch), consistent with the other German glosses Wirbel and Mahlstrom.
'ee.' after 'not easy to explain' is probably 'cc.' or '&c.' (an etc.-type abbreviation introducing the list of names).
'With the regard to' is likely Riemann's slip for Brewster's 'With regard to'.
